technical.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python, and when would you pick each?
technical.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable, so you can change, append to, or remove items from a list but not from a tuple. Because tuples cannot change, they can be used as dictionary keys or set members when all their items are hashable. Use a list for a collection that grows or changes, like rows read from a file. Use a tuple for a fixed record, like a (latitude, longitude) pair or a function returning several values.

technical.q: What is a generator in Python and why would you use one when processing a large file?
technical.answer: A generator is a function that uses yield to produce values one at a time instead of building a full list in memory. It keeps its state between calls and resumes where it left off. When reading a large file line by line, a generator lets you process each line and discard it, so memory use stays small. The trade-off is that a generator can be iterated only once and does not support indexing or len.

technical.q: Explain NumPy broadcasting with an example.
technical.answer: Broadcasting is the rule that lets NumPy combine arrays of different shapes by stretching dimensions of size 1 to match the other array. Shapes are compared from the last dimension backward, and each pair must be equal or one of them must be 1. For example, adding a vector of shape (3,) to a matrix of shape (2, 3) adds the vector to each row. It avoids explicit loops and does not make full copies of the smaller array.

technical.q: You have a pandas DataFrame of chat logs with user_id, timestamp and token_count. How do you get total tokens per user per day?
technical.answer: First convert the timestamp column with pd.to_datetime, then create a date column with dt.date or use pd.Grouper with a daily frequency. Then call groupby on user_id and the date, select token_count, and call sum. Use reset_index to turn the result back into a flat DataFrame. For very large data, check dtypes and consider reading in chunks or using a columnar format like Parquet.

technical.q: How does asyncio help when your app calls an LLM API for many requests, and what are its limits?
technical.answer: Calling an LLM API is mostly waiting on network I/O, so asyncio lets one thread start many requests and switch between them while each waits. You write async functions, use an async HTTP or SDK client, and run them together with asyncio.gather or a task group. It does not speed up CPU-heavy work, because the event loop runs on a single thread. You should also cap concurrency, for example with a semaphore, to respect provider rate limits.

technical.q: What is the GIL and how does it affect threads versus processes for ML workloads?
technical.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock in standard CPython lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for I/O-bound work because the lock is released while waiting. For CPU-bound pure Python code, you use multiprocessing so each process has its own interpreter. Many numeric libraries like NumPy do heavy work in native code that can release the lock, so threads can help there too.

technical.q: What does the dot product of two vectors measure, and why does it matter in embeddings?
technical.answer: The dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them, and it grows when two vectors point in a similar direction. It equals the product of the two lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. If vectors are normalized to length 1, the dot product equals cosine similarity. This is why vector search often uses dot product or cosine similarity to find embeddings that are close in meaning.

technical.q: What is a gradient and why does gradient descent use it?
technical.answer: A gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of a function, one per input, and it points in the direction of steepest increase. To minimize a loss, gradient descent moves the parameters a small step in the opposite direction of the gradient. The step size is set by the learning rate. Repeating this many times moves the parameters toward a low loss, though not always a global minimum.

technical.q: How does the chain rule relate to backpropagation?
technical.answer: The chain rule says the derivative of a composed function is the product of the derivatives of its parts. A neural network is a composition of layers, so the gradient of the loss with respect to an early weight is a product of local derivatives along the path from the loss back to that weight. Backpropagation computes these products efficiently by going from the output backward and reusing intermediate results. This is what automatic differentiation in frameworks does for you.

technical.q: State Bayes rule and give a simple example of where it matters.
technical.answer: Bayes rule says P(A given B) equals P(B given A) times P(A) divided by P(B). It lets you update a belief about A after seeing evidence B. A classic example is a medical test: even a fairly accurate test can give mostly false positives when the disease is rare, because the prior P(A) is small. The same idea sits behind Naive Bayes classifiers.

technical.q: What does softmax do, and why is it paired with cross-entropy loss for classification?
technical.answer: Softmax turns a vector of raw scores called logits into positive numbers that sum to 1, so they can be read as class probabilities. Cross-entropy loss measures how much probability the model puts on the true class, and it is the negative log of that probability. The pair works well because the gradient with respect to the logits is simply the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target. In code, implementations combine them for numerical stability.

technical.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
technical.answer: Bias is error from a model being too simple to capture the real pattern, and variance is error from a model being too sensitive to the particular training sample. A very simple model has high bias and underfits, while a very flexible model has high variance and overfits. Expected test error combines bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. You manage the trade-off with model complexity, regularization, more data, and cross-validation.

technical.q: Why do we split data into training, validation and test sets?
technical.answer: The training set is used to fit the model parameters. The validation set is used to compare models and tune hyperparameters, so it guides your choices. The test set is held back until the end to give an unbiased estimate of performance on new data. If you tune on the test set, its score becomes optimistic because you have indirectly fit to it.

technical.q: Explain precision and recall. When would you favor one over the other?
technical.answer: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are truly positive, and recall is the share of actual positives that the model finds. Favor recall when missing a positive is costly, such as screening for a serious disease or fraud triage. Favor precision when false alarms are costly, such as auto-blocking user accounts. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the two, and moving the decision threshold trades one for the other.

technical.q: How do you detect and reduce overfitting?
technical.answer: You detect it when training performance is strong but validation performance is clearly worse, or when validation loss starts rising while training loss keeps falling. To reduce it, you can get more or better data, simplify the model, add regularization such as L2 or dropout, use early stopping, and apply data augmentation where it fits. Cross-validation gives a more reliable signal on small datasets. Also check for data leakage, which can mislead you in the opposite direction.

technical.q: Compare random forests and gradient boosted trees.
technical.answer: A random forest trains many deep trees independently on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and averages them, which mainly reduces variance. Gradient boosting trains trees one after another, each fitting the errors of the ensemble so far, which mainly reduces bias. Boosting often reaches higher accuracy on tabular data but is more sensitive to hyperparameters and can overfit if not tuned. Random forests are easier to train and are robust with default settings.

technical.q: You are building a classifier where only 1 percent of examples are positive. How do you approach it?
technical.answer: First choose metrics that fit, such as precision, recall, PR-AUC or F1, instead of accuracy. Then consider class weights in the loss, resampling such as oversampling the minority class only within training data, and threshold tuning based on the business cost of each error. Use stratified splits so each fold keeps the class ratio. Always check on an untouched test set with the real class distribution.

technical.q: Why and when do you scale features?
technical.answer: Scaling puts features on comparable ranges, which matters for models that use distances or gradients, such as k-nearest neighbors, SVMs, linear models with regularization, and neural networks. Tree-based models are largely unaffected because they split on thresholds. Common choices are standardization to zero mean and unit variance, or min-max scaling. Fit the scaler on the training data only and apply it to validation and test data to avoid leakage.

technical.q: Explain how a neural network learns, from forward pass to weight update.
technical.answer: In the forward pass, inputs flow through layers of weighted sums and nonlinear activations to produce a prediction. A loss function compares the prediction with the target. Backpropagation then computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using the chain rule. An optimizer such as SGD or Adam uses those gradients to update the weights, and this repeats over many batches and epochs.

technical.q: Why is ReLU popular, and what problems can it have?
technical.answer: ReLU outputs max(0, x), which is cheap to compute and has a gradient of 1 for positive inputs, so it helps avoid the vanishing gradient problem seen with sigmoid and tanh in deep networks. Its problem is dead neurons: if a neuron's input stays negative, its gradient is zero and it may stop learning. Variants such as Leaky ReLU, GELU and SiLU address this. GELU is common in transformer models.

technical.q: What is the difference between batch normalization and layer normalization, and why do transformers use layer norm?
technical.answer: Batch normalization normalizes each feature using statistics computed across the batch, while layer normalization normalizes across the features of a single example. Batch norm depends on batch size and behaves differently in training and inference. Layer norm has no dependence on other examples, so it works with small batches and variable-length sequences. That makes it a natural fit for transformers.

technical.q: How does dropout work and what happens at inference time?
technical.answer: During training, dropout randomly sets a fraction of activations to zero on each forward pass, which discourages neurons from relying too heavily on each other and reduces overfitting. The remaining activations are scaled so the expected output stays consistent. At inference, dropout is turned off and all units are used. In frameworks, this is why you switch between train and eval modes.

technical.q: How does Adam differ from plain SGD, and what does AdamW change?
technical.answer: SGD updates weights using the current gradient scaled by a learning rate, optionally with momentum. Adam keeps running averages of the gradient and of its square, so it adapts the step size for each parameter. AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient update, which gives cleaner regularization than adding an L2 term to the loss inside Adam. AdamW is a common default for training transformers, usually with a learning rate warmup and decay schedule.

technical.q: What causes vanishing and exploding gradients and how do you deal with them?
technical.answer: In deep networks or long sequences, backpropagation multiplies many local derivatives, and if these are mostly smaller than 1 the gradient shrinks toward zero, while if they are larger than 1 it can blow up. Vanishing gradients stop early layers from learning, and exploding gradients cause unstable training. Remedies include ReLU-family activations, careful weight initialization, normalization layers, residual connections, and gradient clipping for the exploding case. Gated architectures like LSTMs were designed partly to address this in sequences.

technical.q: Explain self-attention in a transformer in plain terms.
technical.answer: Each token is turned into three vectors called query, key and value by learned linear projections. A token's query is compared with every token's key using a dot product, scaled and passed through softmax, to get attention weights. Those weights are used to take a weighted average of the value vectors, so each token's new representation mixes in information from the tokens it finds relevant. This lets the model relate any two positions in a sequence directly.

technical.q: Why do transformers need positional information?
technical.answer: Self-attention treats its input as a set, so on its own it has no sense of word order. Without position information, two sentences with the same words in a different order would look the same to the attention layers. The original transformer added sinusoidal position encodings to the token embeddings. Many modern models use other schemes, such as rotary position embeddings, that inject relative position into the attention computation.

technical.q: What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers? Give examples.
technical.answer: Encoder-only models like BERT read the whole input with bidirectional attention and are used for understanding tasks such as classification and embeddings. Decoder-only models like the GPT family use causal attention, where each token sees only earlier tokens, and generate text one token at a time. Encoder-decoder models like T5 encode an input and then decode an output that attends to it, suited to translation and summarization. Most current chat LLMs are decoder-only.

technical.q: What is a KV cache and why does it matter for LLM inference?
technical.answer: When generating token by token, the keys and values of earlier tokens do not change, so the model stores them and reuses them instead of recomputing them at every step. Each new token then only needs its own query, key and value computed and attended against the cached ones. This makes generation much faster but uses GPU memory that grows with sequence length, batch size and model size. It is a main reason long contexts and many concurrent users are memory bound.

technical.q: What is the computational cost of self-attention with sequence length, and how is it reduced in practice?
technical.answer: Standard self-attention compares every token with every other token, so time and memory for the attention matrix grow quadratically with sequence length. This limits long contexts. FlashAttention computes exact attention with a memory-efficient tiled algorithm that avoids writing the full matrix to slow GPU memory. Other approaches include sparse or sliding-window attention and sharing keys and values across heads to reduce cache cost.

technical.q: What is tokenization and why do LLMs use subword tokens?
technical.answer: Tokenization splits text into units called tokens, which the model maps to integer IDs and then to embeddings. Subword methods like byte-pair encoding keep common words as single tokens and split rare words into smaller pieces. This keeps the vocabulary a manageable size while still being able to represent any word, including new or misspelled ones. Tokens are also the unit for context limits and API billing, so token counts matter for cost.

technical.q: What makes a good prompt for a production LLM feature?
technical.answer: A good prompt states the task and role clearly, gives the needed context, specifies the output format, and includes a few examples when the format or style is tricky. For structured output, ask for a schema and validate the result in code. Keep instructions specific and separate instructions from user-provided data to reduce injection risk. Then test the prompt against a set of saved cases rather than judging by a few tries, and version it like code.

technical.q: What do temperature and top-p do, and how would you set them for a data-extraction task?
technical.answer: Temperature rescales the model's token probabilities before sampling: lower values make the output more deterministic and higher values make it more varied. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. For extraction or classification, you usually want a low temperature so results are consistent. For brainstorming or creative writing, a higher value is more suitable.

technical.q: When would you fine-tune a model instead of using prompting or RAG?
technical.answer: Start with prompting because it is cheapest to iterate on. Use RAG when the model needs fresh, private or large amounts of factual knowledge, since retrieval can be updated without retraining. Fine-tuning fits when you need a consistent style, format or behavior, or want a smaller model to match a larger one on a narrow task, and you have good labeled examples. Fine-tuning is not a reliable way to add lots of new facts, and it adds cost for data, training and maintenance.

technical.q: What is hallucination in LLMs and how do you reduce it in an application?
technical.answer: Hallucination is when a model produces fluent text that is false or not supported by the source. To reduce it in an app, ground answers in retrieved documents, instruct the model to answer only from the context and to say when it does not know, and ask for citations. You can also add output validation, use lower temperature for factual tasks, and add human review for high-stakes cases. You cannot eliminate it fully, so measure it with an evaluation set.

technical.q: How do you get reliable structured JSON output from an LLM?
technical.answer: Use the provider's structured output or function calling feature when available, which constrains the response to a JSON schema. Otherwise, describe the schema in the prompt with an example. In either case, parse and validate the output with a schema library in your code, and handle failures with a retry that includes the error message. Keep schemas simple, with clear field descriptions, because complex or ambiguous schemas increase errors.

technical.q: What is a context window and how do you handle conversations that exceed it?
technical.answer: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can take in and produce in one request, including the prompt, history and output. When a conversation grows past it, or gets expensive, you can trim the oldest turns, summarize earlier turns into a short note, or store facts externally and retrieve them when needed. Keep the system prompt and the most recent turns intact. Longer contexts also cost more and can make it harder for the model to use details buried in the middle.

technical.q: What is RAG and what problem does it solve?
technical.answer: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant documents for a user's question and puts them into the prompt so the model answers from that context. It helps the model use private, recent or domain-specific information that it was not trained on, and it lets you show sources. The basic pipeline is: split documents into chunks, embed and index them, retrieve the top matches for a query, then generate an answer from them. Answer quality depends heavily on retrieval quality.

technical.q: How do you choose a chunking strategy for a RAG system?
technical.answer: Chunks should be small enough to be specific and fit several in the prompt, but large enough to keep a complete idea. A common start is a few hundred tokens with some overlap, split on natural boundaries such as headings or paragraphs. Keep metadata such as title, section and source with each chunk. Then tune chunk size by measuring retrieval on a set of real questions rather than guessing.

technical.q: How do embeddings and vector search work together in retrieval?
technical.answer: An embedding model turns text into a vector so that texts with similar meaning are close together. You embed each chunk once and store the vectors in an index. At query time you embed the question with the same model and find the nearest vectors by cosine similarity or dot product. For large collections, approximate nearest neighbor indexes such as HNSW trade a little accuracy for much faster search.

technical.q: What are hybrid search and reranking, and why use them?
technical.answer: Hybrid search combines keyword search such as BM25 with vector search, so you catch both exact terms and semantic matches, and results are merged with a method like reciprocal rank fusion. Reranking takes the top candidates, for example the top 50, and rescores them with a cross-encoder or similar model that reads the query and each passage together, which is more accurate but slower. The usual pattern is a fast first-stage retrieval followed by a slower reranker on a small set. Both often improve relevance over plain vector search.

technical.q: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
technical.answer: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For retrieval, build a set of questions with known relevant documents and measure metrics such as recall at k or mean reciprocal rank. For generation, check whether the answer is faithful to the retrieved context and whether it actually answers the question, using human review or an LLM judge that you have checked against human labels. Also track latency, cost and the rate of correct refusals when the answer is not in the documents.

technical.q: Users say the RAG bot gives wrong answers. How do you debug it?
technical.answer: Take failing examples and check the retrieved chunks first: if the right passage was not retrieved, the problem is retrieval, such as chunking, embeddings, missing keyword matching or metadata filters. If the right passage was retrieved but the answer is wrong, the problem is generation, such as prompt instructions, too much noisy context, or the passage being ambiguous. Also check whether the source documents are outdated or missing. Fix the layer at fault, then add the failing cases to the evaluation set to prevent regressions.

technical.q: What is an LLM agent and how is it different from a simple LLM call?
technical.answer: An agent uses an LLM in a loop: the model decides what to do next, calls tools such as search or an API, sees the results, and continues until it finishes or hits a limit. A simple LLM call takes input and returns text once. Agents are useful when the steps are not known in advance, but they are slower, costlier and less predictable. If a fixed workflow of steps solves the problem, that is often simpler and more reliable.

technical.q: How does function calling or tool use work?
technical.answer: You give the model a list of tools, each with a name, description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model decides a tool is needed, it returns a structured request naming the tool and its arguments instead of a final answer. Your code runs the tool, then sends the result back to the model as a new message, and the model continues. The model never executes anything itself, so your code controls what actually runs.

technical.q: Describe the ReAct pattern.
technical.answer: ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting: the model reasons about what to do, takes an action such as calling a tool, observes the result, and repeats until it can answer. The observations ground the next reasoning step in real data instead of guesses. It is a simple loop that underlies many agent frameworks. Its weaknesses include compounding errors over many steps, cost from many model calls, and the need for a step limit.

technical.q: How do you make an agent that can take actions, like sending email or changing records, safe?
technical.answer: Give it the least privilege it needs, with narrowly scoped tools and permissions tied to the end user. Require human confirmation for irreversible or high-impact actions, validate all tool arguments in code, and rate limit and log every call. Treat any text the agent reads from documents or web pages as untrusted, since it may contain prompt injection that tries to trigger actions. Add step and budget limits, and test with adversarial cases.

technical.q: How would you give an agent memory across sessions?
technical.answer: Separate short-term memory, which is the current conversation in the context window, from long-term memory stored outside the model. For long-term memory, save useful facts or summaries to a database or vector store with user ID and timestamps, and retrieve relevant items at the start of or during a session. Decide what is worth saving, since storing everything adds noise and privacy risk. Allow users to view and delete stored memories.

technical.q: When is a multi-agent setup worth it versus a single agent?
technical.answer: Start with a single agent or a simple workflow, since every extra agent adds cost, latency and places for errors to compound. Multiple agents can help when tasks split into distinct roles with different tools or prompts, when context would otherwise get too crowded, or when work can run in parallel. A common design is one coordinator that delegates to specialized workers. You should compare it against the single-agent baseline on an evaluation set before committing.
followUps: How do agents pass information to each other?
How do you debug a failure in a multi-agent run?
technical.weak: Assumes more agents is always better without a baseline comparison.

technical.q: How would you deploy a trained model as an API?
technical.answer: Wrap the model in a web service, for example with FastAPI, that loads the model once at startup and exposes a prediction endpoint with validated input and output schemas. Package it in a Docker container so the environment is reproducible, and deploy it on a platform that can scale replicas behind a load balancer. Add health checks, logging, and timeouts. For heavy models, consider batching requests and using GPUs or a dedicated serving framework.
followUps: Why load the model at startup rather than per request?
How would you roll out a new model version safely?
technical.weak: Says just run the script on a server and does not mention packaging, validation or scaling.

technical.q: What should you monitor for a model in production and what is drift?
technical.answer: Monitor system metrics like latency, error rate and cost, and model quality metrics like accuracy on labeled samples or user feedback. Drift means the data or the relationship between inputs and outputs changes over time, so the model performs worse than it did at training. Data drift is a change in input distribution, while concept drift is a change in what the correct output is for a given input. Alerts on these signals should trigger investigation, and possibly retraining.
followUps: How can you detect drift when you have no labels?
What would trigger a retraining run?
technical.weak: Monitors only uptime and latency, with nothing about the quality of predictions.

technical.q: Why track experiments and version data and models?
technical.answer: To reproduce a result you need to know the code version, data version, hyperparameters and environment that produced it. Experiment tracking tools record parameters, metrics and artifacts for each run so you can compare runs and go back to a good one. A model registry stores versioned models with their stage, such as staging or production. Without this, teams cannot explain why a model changed or roll back reliably.
followUps: What would you record for each training run?
How do you version large datasets?
technical.weak: Saves models with names like final_v2 and cannot reproduce how they were made.

technical.q: How is CI/CD for a machine learning or LLM app different from a normal web app?
technical.answer: Besides testing code, you also need to test data and model behavior, since a change in a prompt, model version or data can change outputs without any code error. A pipeline can run unit tests, then an evaluation suite on a fixed dataset with score thresholds that block deployment if quality drops. Deploy gradually with canary or shadow traffic and keep a fast rollback path. Version prompts, models and configs alongside code.
followUps: How would you set a threshold on a non-deterministic eval?
What is shadow deployment?
technical.weak: Treats it like a standard web deploy and adds no evaluation gate.

technical.q: How would you reduce latency and cost of an LLM feature in production?
technical.answer: Cut tokens by trimming prompts and context, and cache repeated requests or use provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes. Route simple requests to a smaller, cheaper model and reserve the large model for hard ones. Stream the response so users see output sooner, and set a maximum output length. Track cost and latency per request so you can see which features drive them, and check quality with your evaluation set after each change.
followUps: What is the risk of a semantic cache?
How would you decide which requests go to the small model?
technical.weak: Just switches to a cheaper model without measuring the effect on quality.

technical.q: What is batching in model inference and what is the trade-off?
technical.answer: Batching processes several requests together so the GPU does more work per pass, which raises throughput and lowers cost per request. The trade-off is latency, because a request may wait for others to fill the batch. For LLMs, continuous batching lets new requests join a running batch as others finish, which improves utilization compared with fixed batches. You tune batch size and wait time against your latency target.
followUps: Why is memory often the limit for batch size with LLMs?
What is quantization and how does it help serving?
technical.weak: Says bigger batches are always better and ignores the effect on latency.

design.q: Design a RAG-based customer support bot over 10,000 help documents.
clarify: What are the languages, document formats, and how often do documents change?
What are the latency, traffic and accuracy targets, and what happens when the bot is unsure?
Is the content public or does it have access restrictions, and are there compliance needs?
approach: Ingest: parse documents, clean them, split into chunks by headings with overlap, and attach metadata such as title, product and date.
Index: embed chunks and store them in a vector index alongside a keyword index for hybrid search.
Retrieve: run hybrid search for the query, then rerank the top candidates to a small set.
Generate: prompt the model to answer only from the retrieved passages, cite sources, and say so when the answer is not found.
Fallback: hand off to a human agent or ticket when confidence is low or the user asks.
Evaluate: build a test set of real questions, measure retrieval recall and answer faithfulness, and re-run on every change.
Operate: log queries and retrieved chunks, collect thumbs up or down, and set up incremental re-indexing when documents change.
tradeoffs: Larger chunks give more context but lower precision and higher token cost.
Reranking improves relevance but adds latency and cost.
A stricter refusal policy reduces wrong answers but increases unanswered questions.
mistakes: Skipping evaluation and tuning by trying a few questions by hand.
Not planning for document updates, so answers go stale.

design.q: Design an agent that books meetings for users by email or chat.
clarify: Which calendars and email systems must it support, and what permissions will users grant?
Can it act alone or must users approve before invites are sent?
How should it handle time zones, conflicts and people outside the organization?
approach: Define tools: read availability, create event, update event, send message, and look up contacts, each with a strict argument schema.
Authenticate with per-user OAuth scopes limited to what is needed.
Run a loop where the model proposes times from availability and the tool results, with a step limit.
Validate all arguments in code, including time zone handling and attendee lists.
Require user confirmation before creating or sending anything visible to others, at least at first.
Log every tool call and decision for audit and debugging.
Test with a set of scripted scenarios such as conflicts, ambiguous times and cancellations.
tradeoffs: More autonomy saves user effort but raises the risk of wrong or embarrassing actions.
A fixed workflow is more predictable, while a free agent loop handles unusual requests better.
Broad calendar permissions make it more capable but increase privacy and security exposure.
mistakes: Letting the model output raw times without explicit time zone handling and validation.
Treating incoming email text as trusted, which opens the door to prompt injection.

design.q: Design cost control for an LLM feature in a multi-tenant SaaS product.
clarify: What are the pricing plans and do customers have usage quotas?
Which features use LLMs and how sensitive are they to quality and latency?
Do we need per-customer cost reporting or hard limits?
approach: Meter every call: record tenant, feature, model, input tokens, output tokens and cost.
Set per-tenant budgets and rate limits, with soft warnings and hard stops.
Reduce tokens with prompt trimming, context limits and max output length.
Cache repeated requests and use provider prompt caching for shared long prefixes.
Route by difficulty: use a smaller model for simple tasks and escalate to a larger one when needed.
Build dashboards and alerts for spend spikes and anomalies by tenant.
Re-run the evaluation set after each cost change to confirm quality holds.
tradeoffs: Hard limits protect margins but can hurt user experience at the limit.
Model routing saves money but adds complexity and a risk of wrong routing.
Caching cuts cost but can serve stale or wrong answers if keys are too loose.
mistakes: Tracking only the total monthly bill, so no one knows which tenant or feature causes it.
Downgrading the model to save money without measuring quality.

design.q: Design an evaluation pipeline for an LLM application that changes often.
clarify: What does good mean for this app: correctness, format, tone, safety, or a mix?
Do we have real user data or labeled examples to start from?
How fast must results come back on each change, and what is the budget for evaluation runs?
approach: Collect a dataset of representative inputs from real logs, plus edge cases and known past failures.
Define metrics per task: exact checks where possible, rubrics or an LLM judge for open-ended quality.
Calibrate any LLM judge against a sample of human labels.
Run the suite automatically in CI on every prompt, model or retrieval change and compare against the current baseline.
Set score thresholds that block release and report regressions by category.
Monitor production with sampled traces and user feedback, and feed new failures back into the dataset.
Version the dataset, prompts and results so runs are comparable over time.
tradeoffs: Human labels are accurate but slow and costly, while LLM judges are fast but can be biased.
A large suite gives more coverage but takes longer and costs more per run.
Strict thresholds catch regressions but can block changes because of noise in scores.
mistakes: Using a tiny hand-picked set that does not reflect real traffic.
Trusting an LLM judge without checking its agreement with humans.

design.q: Design a document Q&A system where users may only see documents they have permission to access.
clarify: What is the source of permissions, such as an identity provider or the source system's access lists, and how often do they change?
How many users, documents and tenants are there, and how sensitive is the data?
Do answers need citations and audit logs?
approach: Ingest documents with their access metadata, such as owner, groups and tenant, stored with every chunk.
Sync permission changes from the source system on a schedule or by events, and handle document deletion.
At query time, identify the user and their groups, and apply an access filter inside the retrieval query itself.
Only pass chunks the user is allowed to see to the model, so restricted text never enters the prompt.
Generate an answer with citations that link only to accessible documents.
Log queries, retrieved chunks and access decisions for audit.
Test with cases where users try to reach documents they should not, including through crafted questions.
tradeoffs: Filtering inside the search is safest but can constrain which index types you can use and adds complexity.
Frequent permission syncing is more accurate but costs more than periodic syncing.
A separate index per tenant gives strong isolation but is costlier to run than a shared index with filters.
mistakes: Retrieving first and filtering after generation, which can leak restricted content.
Ignoring permission changes after ingestion, so removed users still get answers.

design.q: Design a chat feature with streamed responses and rate limits for a web app.
clarify: How many concurrent users do we expect and what are the latency targets?
Are there usage plans with different limits, and should limits apply to requests, tokens or both?
Do conversations need to be saved and resumed?
approach: Build a backend endpoint that calls the LLM with streaming enabled and forwards chunks to the browser using server-sent events or WebSockets.
Render tokens progressively on the client and support cancel and retry.
Store messages in a database with conversation IDs so history can be reloaded.
Apply rate limits per user and per plan using a shared store such as Redis, counting both requests and tokens.
Handle upstream errors and provider rate limits with retries, backoff and a clear message to the user.
Trim or summarize history to stay within the context window and cost budget.
Add moderation and logging, and monitor time to first token and error rate.
tradeoffs: Streaming improves perceived speed but makes validating or moderating the full answer before display harder.
Token-based limits match cost better than request counts but are harder to explain to users.
Server-sent events are simpler than WebSockets, while WebSockets suit two-way needs.
mistakes: Not handling client disconnects, so the server keeps generating and paying for tokens nobody sees.
Limiting only by request count, so a few very long requests bypass the intended cost limits.

behavioral.q: Why are you moving from web development to AI engineering?
behavioral.tip: Use a short story: what you were doing, the moment or project that pulled you toward AI, and what you did about it. Emphasize that your web experience is an asset because AI apps still need APIs, data handling and reliable products.
behavioral.example: Situation: at [company or project] I built [web feature]. Task: users needed [problem an LLM could help with]. Action: I learned [skill], built [small project], and measured [result]. Result: [outcome], which showed me I want to do this full time, using my [web strength] to ship dependable products.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a hard bug you debugged.
behavioral.tip: Walk through your method in STAR steps: how you reproduced it, narrowed it down, and confirmed the fix. Highlight logging and hypothesis testing, which apply directly to debugging model and pipeline behavior.
behavioral.example: Situation: [system] showed [symptom]. Task: find the cause under [constraint]. Action: I reproduced it by [step], added [logs or tests], ruled out [causes], and found [root cause]. Result: fixed by [change], added [test or monitor] so it would not return.

behavioral.q: Describe a time you had to learn a new technology quickly.
behavioral.tip: Show a repeatable learning method: pick a small goal, build something, get feedback. As a career changer, use a recent AI or ML example to show you can keep learning.
behavioral.example: Situation: [project] required [new tool]. Task: be productive within [time]. Action: I read [source], built [small prototype], asked [person or community], and applied it to [real task]. Result: delivered [outcome] and documented [notes] for others.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate and how you handled it.
behavioral.tip: Focus on listening, using data or a small experiment to resolve the question, and keeping the relationship intact. Avoid blaming the other person.
behavioral.example: Situation: [teammate] and I disagreed on [decision]. Task: choose the best option for [goal]. Action: I listened to [their view], proposed [test or data], and we compared [criteria]. Result: we chose [option], and [outcome or lesson].

behavioral.q: Tell me about a project with unclear requirements.
behavioral.tip: Show how you turned vagueness into a plan: clarifying questions, a small first version, and feedback loops. This matters a lot in AI work, where the right answer is often unclear at the start.
behavioral.example: Situation: [stakeholder] asked for [vague goal]. Task: deliver something useful. Action: I asked about [users and success criteria], built [small first version], and gathered [feedback]. Result: we refined it into [outcome] and defined [metric] to track success.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a mistake.
behavioral.tip: Pick a real, modest failure, own it briefly, and spend most of the answer on what you changed afterward. Interviewers look for honesty and a concrete lesson, not a perfect record.
behavioral.example: Situation: on [project] I [mistake]. Task: fix the impact and prevent repeats. Action: I told [people], fixed [issue], and added [process, test or check]. Result: [outcome], and I now [changed habit].

behavioral.q: Tell me about a project you are proud of and its impact.
behavioral.tip: Pick a project where you can state your own role and a result, ideally a number or a clear before and after. If it is a personal AI project, explain what you measured and how you improved it.
behavioral.example: Situation: [project context]. Task: my part was [role and goal]. Action: I [key technical choices] and [how you tested or measured]. Result: [metric or user outcome], and I learned [lesson].

behavioral.q: Explain a complex technical idea to a non-technical person.
behavioral.tip: Show that you start from the listener's need, use a simple analogy, and check understanding. Communication with non-technical stakeholders is a strong skill to highlight from web work.
behavioral.example: Situation: [stakeholder] needed to understand [concept or decision]. Task: help them decide. Action: I used [analogy], showed [simple example or demo], and checked with [question]. Result: they [decision or understanding], and we [outcome].
